title: Reduce streaming token latency: kernel scheduling, KV cache, continuous batching, and backpressure tuning
author: Alicia Chen
description: Motivation: Streaming token latency (1-99th percentile token arrival time) is a critical SLO for realtime LLM features. Workloads hitting small prompt sizes or high concurrency have seen elevated per-token tail latency due to suboptimal kernel scheduling, inefficient KV cache access patterns on cache hits, conservative flush cadence for the streaming token loop, and aggressive backpressure that serialized batches. This PR bundles targeted changes across the serving runtime to reduce end-to-end streaming token latency without increasing overall GPU utilization. What I changed (single continuous description): - Kernel scheduling: introduce a prioritized micro-batching scheduler that prefers in-progress token loops with non-empty KV cache to reduce stalls from kernel warm-ups. This adds a lightweight priority queue and a short-circuit path for hot KV-cache requests. - KV cache: refactor KV cache read path to use a contiguous read buffer with prefetch hints and reduced locking for read-mostly flows. Add a fast-path for single-token continuation requests that avoids the full cache reconciliation. - Continuous batching / flush cadence: tune the token loop flush cadence to allow sub-2ms flush opportunities when packets are small and latency SLOs are strict; add adaptive cadence heuristic based on observed inter-arrival times. - Backpressure / flow control: relax conservative upstream backpressure thresholds when the scheduler detects cached KV hits and low GPU queue depth; implement a bounded speculative batching window to avoid serializing single-request streams. - Tests & instrumentation: add microbenchmarks, end-to-end streaming latency tests, and new tracing tags for scheduler decisions, KV cache hit/hint metrics, and flush events. Update dashboards to expose token-level p50/p90/p99 after this change. Implementation notes: The change touches the kernel_scheduler, kv_cache, batcher, and token_streamer components. I kept the interfaces backward-compatible: no external RPC surface changes. All new heuristics are opt-in via runtime flags for safe rollout to Dedicated clusters. The scheduler change is implemented as a non-blocking priority queue with per-worker windows to avoid global contention. KV cache refactor maintains the same eviction semantics. Performance: On our internal perf-canary harness (gpt-medium workload, 4k clients, mixed prompt lengths): median token latency improved ~14%, p95 improved ~26%, p99 improved ~32%. For small prompt workloads (<64 tokens) observed ~40% reduction in first-token latency due to faster KV cache fast-path and reduced kernel warm-up. GPU throughput remained within 3% of baseline. Rollout plan: Feature gated. Start canary on Dedicated pool (staging) for 48h, then ramp to 10% of production host pools. Monitor token-level SLOs, GPU utilization, and 'speculative_batch_miss' traces. Revert flag available to quickly disable priority scheduling if adverse behavior observed. Related: ENG-9876 (streaming latency initiative), ENG-10012 (kv-cache refactor), related PRs: pr-48901, pr-50748 for earlier backpressure fixes. Notes: kept description as a single continuous string per repo conventions.
commits:
6 commits:
1) kernel_scheduler: add prioritized micro-batch queue and worker windowing
2) kv_cache: contiguous read buffer + single-token fast-path
3) batcher: speculative batching window and adaptive flush cadence
4) token_streamer: integrate cadence heuristics and tracing hooks
5) tests: add streaming_latency_test and microbench harness updates
6) docs: release notes and rollout instructions
